item.research_question: How do crystal orientation, temperature, and strain rate affect the mechanical properties and plastic deformation mechanisms of an equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy?
item.material_system: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy (Co-free variant of the Cantor alloy)
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS software with Embedded-atom method (EAM) potential; model size 108.3 Å × 108.3 Å × 180.5 Å (180,000 atoms); relaxation via heating to 1000 K and cooling to 300 K; tensile loading at temperatures of 10 K, 300 K, 600 K and strain rates of 10^8 s^-1, 10^9 s^-1, 10^10 s^-1 along <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> orientations.
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile loading; temperatures: 10 K, 300 K, 600 K; strain rates: 10^8 s^-1, 10^9 s^-1, 10^10 s^-1; crystal orientations: <110>, <1-12>, <-111>; time step: 1 fs; periodic boundary conditions.
key_findings: The <-111> orientation exhibited the highest yield strength and elastic modulus due to atomic close-packing along (111) planes.
Yield strength and yield strain decreased significantly as temperature increased from 10 K to 600 K.
Dislocation density decreased with increasing temperature due to enhanced atomic mobility and dislocation annihilation.
Yield strength was relatively insensitive to strain rate variations (10^8 to 10^10 s^-1) within the simulated range.
Higher strain rates resulted in higher dislocation densities and elevated flow stress after yielding.
Dislocation nucleation primarily occurred at vacancy sites formed by disordered atoms during early deformation stages.
No FCC-to-BCC phase transformation was observed; HCP atoms were attributed to stacking faults rather than true phase transformation.
Shockley partial dislocations and stair-rod immobile dislocations were the primary dislocation types mediating plastic deformation.
item.mechanism: The authors explain that elevated temperatures intensify atomic thermal vibrations, weakening bonding forces and lowering the critical resolved shear stress, which facilitates dislocation nucleation and motion, thereby reducing yield strength. Conversely, higher strain rates do not significantly affect yield strength but increase flow stress by generating higher dislocation densities due to insufficient time for dislocation annihilation or cross-slip, leading to dislocation accumulation and strengthening.
item.limitations: The study was conducted at the nanoscale with relatively small variations in strain rates, which may limit the generalizability of the strain rate insensitivity finding; no significant deformation twins were observed, likely due to high twinning nucleation energy under the specific simulation conditions.
item.future_work: The authors propose conducting related experiments to explore twinning behavior during annealing and comparing preliminary experimental results with simulation findings to distinguish between deformation twins and annealing twins.
quotes: The results revealed that the FeNiCrMn HEA exhibited significant anisotropy under loading along different orientations, with the maximum yield stress observed along the <11-1> direction.
Elevated temperatures intensify atomic thermal vibrations, making it easier for atoms to deviate from their equilibrium positions and facilitating dislocation nucleation and movement.
Higher strain rates correspond to instantaneous dislocation density strengthening, which leads to higher flow stress.
